title: Split coordinates for a chart, its characteristic chart and monoid ideals
statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $M$ an integral commutative monoid (its map to its group completion is injective), with a homomorphism $\beta:M\to(A,\cdot)$ identifying $\beta^{-1}(A^\times)$ with $A^\times$; write $\iota:A^\times\to M$ for the inverse on units. Let $P$ be fine saturated [def-trf-fs-log-blowup] and $a_M:P\to M$ a chart in the following algebraic sense: for $\alpha=\beta a_M$ and $F=\alpha^{-1}(A^\times)$, the map $P\oplus_F A^\times\to M$, $[p,e]\mapsto a_M(p)\iota(e)$, is an isomorphism. Here the pushout identifies $(p+f,e)$ with $(p,\alpha(f)e)$. Put $P_F=\{p-f:p\in P,f\in F\}\subset P^{\rm gp}$, $G=F^{\rm gp}$ and $Q=P_F/G$, and choose a monoid section $s:Q\to P_F$. Suppose $b_M:Q\to M$ induces on $M/A^\times$ the same characteristic identification $Q\simeq M/A^\times$ as $a_M$, where quotient means identification of elements differing by a unit. Put $b=\beta b_M$.
Then $F$ is a face, $P_F^\times=G$, and $\alpha$ extends uniquely to $\alpha_F(p-f)=\alpha(p)\alpha(f)^{-1}$. The maps $(q,g)\mapsto s(q)+g$ and $r\mapsto(\bar r,r-s(\bar r))$ are inverse monoid isomorphisms $Q\oplus G\simeq P_F$. The chart extends uniquely to $a_{M,F}:P_F\to M$, and there are isomorphisms $M\simeq P_F\oplus_G A^\times$ and $Q\oplus A^\times\simeq M$, the latter sending $(q,e)$ to $b_M(q)\iota(e)$. There is a unique homomorphism $u:Q\to A^\times$ satisfying $a_{M,F}(s(q))=b_M(q)\iota(u(q))$; in particular, $c(q):=\alpha_F(s(q))=u(q)b(q)$ and $v(g):=\alpha_F(g)$ lies in $A^\times$.
For every monoid ideal $H\subset P$ (including $\varnothing$), meaning $H+P\subset H$, the map $P\to Q$ is surjective, its image $H_x$ of $H$ is an ideal, and $H_F:=\{h-f:h\in H,f\in F\}$ is the inverse image of $H_x$ in $P_F$. Under the displayed splitting, $H_F=H_x\oplus G$. All these maps commute with homomorphisms of the ring and log-monoid data preserving $P,F,s,a_M,b_M$ and the specified characteristic identification.

source.place: Expose VI 1.1--1.2 (printed p. 69), 3.7(a) (printed p. 75); Expose VIII 3.1.1--3.1.5 (printed pp. 98--99). Agent algebraic expansion of chart pushouts and the given section; returned parent steps 1, 2, 4.

proof.text: Use the group-completion and fs conventions of [def-trf-fs-log-blowup]. In a commutative ring, if $xy$ has inverse $z$, then $x(yz)=1$ and $y(xz)=1$. Hence $F$ contains $0$, is closed under addition, and $p+p'\in F$ implies $p,p'\in F$: it is a face. We regard $P$ as a submonoid of $P^{\rm gp}$ by integrality. The subgroup generated by $F$ consists of differences $f-f'$ with $f,f'\in F$, since these differences contain $F$ and are closed under sums and negatives.

source.place: VIII 3.1.2, printed p.98; agent verification of the unit-preimage face

proof.text: Every $g=f-f'\in G$ belongs to $P_F$ together with $-g$, hence is a unit. Conversely, if $r=p-f$ and $-r=p'-f'$ belong to $P_F$, then $p+p'=f+f'\in F$. The face property gives $p,p'\in F$, so $r\in G$. Thus $P_F^\times=G$. Equality $p-f=p'-f'$ means $p+f'=p'+f$ in $P$. Applying $\alpha$ and multiplying by the inverses of $\alpha(f)\alpha(f')$ proves that $\alpha_F(p-f)=\alpha(p)\alpha(f)^{-1}$ is well-defined. Addition of fractions proves multiplicativity, and every extension must take $-f$ to $\alpha(f)^{-1}$; this proves uniqueness.

source.place: VIII 3.1.1--3.1.2, printed p.98; agent fraction calculation

proof.text: Write $\pi:P_F\to Q$ for the quotient. Since $G$ is a group acting by translations, its orbit relation $r\sim r'$ iff $r-r'\in G$ is already a monoid congruence; this is the stated quotient by $G$. As $\pi s=\mathrm{id}$, $r-s(\pi r)\in G$. The two displayed maps in the statement are therefore defined. Their composites are $(q,g)\mapsto(q,s(q)+g-s(q))=(q,g)$ and $r\mapsto s(\pi r)+r-s(\pi r)=r$. Their additivity follows from additivity of $s$ and $\pi$ and subtraction in $P^{\rm gp}$. Thus they are inverse monoid isomorphisms, with no construction or freeness of a section required.

source.place: VIII 3.1.1--3.1.2, printed p.98; agent calculation with the given section

proof.text: For $f\in F$, $a_M(f)=\iota(\alpha(f))$: apply the assumed isomorphism from $\beta^{-1}(A^\times)$ to $A^\times$. Define $\lambda(p-f)=a_M(p)\iota(\alpha(f)^{-1})$. If $p+f'=p'+f$, applying $a_M$ and the preceding equality proves equality of these values after multiplying by unit inverses. Sums of fractions show $\lambda$ is a monoid homomorphism, and the inverse of each $a_M(f)$ is forced, giving uniqueness. Its composite with $\beta$ is $\alpha_F$ by the formula on fractions. For $g\in G$, both $g$ and $-g$ lie in $P_F$, so $\alpha_F(g)\alpha_F(-g)=1$; write $v(g)=\alpha_F(g)\in A^\times$. Then $\lambda(g)=\iota(v(g))$.

source.place: VI 1.1, printed p.69; VIII 3.1.2, printed p.98; agent extension of the chart

proof.text: Put $N=P\oplus_F A^\times$, identified with $M$ by the assumed chart isomorphism. The map $j:P\to N$, $p\mapsto[p,1]$, takes $f\in F$ to $[0,\alpha(f)]$. Thus $j_F(p-f)=[p,\alpha(f)^{-1}]$ is well-defined: if $p+f'=p'+f$, both representatives become $[p+f',\alpha(f+f')^{-1}]$. It is additive and sends $g=f-f'$ to $[0,v(g)]$. Consequently the formulas $[r,e]\mapsto j_F(r)[0,e]$ and $[p,e]\mapsto[p,e]$ induce maps $P_F\oplus_G A^\times\to N$ and $N\to P_F\oplus_G A^\times$ respecting their generating relations. The first composite fixes $[p,e]$; the other sends $[p-f,e]$ to $[p,\alpha(f)^{-1}e]=[p-f,e]$. These inverse maps give $M\simeq P_F\oplus_G A^\times$ with the stated chart extension.

source.place: VI 1.1, printed p.69; VIII 3.1.2, printed p.98; agent explicit pushout comparison

proof.text: Using Step 3, the maps $[r,e]\mapsto(\pi r,v(r-s(\pi r))e)$ and $(q,e)\mapsto[s(q),e]$ identify $P_F\oplus_G A^\times$ with $Q\oplus A^\times$. Indeed replacing $(r+g,e)$ by $(r,v(g)e)$ leaves the first formula unchanged, because $\pi g=0$ and $v$ is multiplicative. The composites are the identity: for the second one, writing $g=r-s(\pi r)$ gives $[s(\pi r),v(g)e]=[s(\pi r)+g,e]=[r,e]$. These formulas also show that the characteristic of $\lambda(r)\iota(e)$ is precisely $\pi r$ under the specified characteristic identification.

source.place: VI 3.7(a), printed p.75; agent calculation of split pushout coordinates

proof.text: By the hypothesis on $b_M$, for every $m\in M$ there is a unique $q\in Q$ with the characteristic class of $m$ equal to that of $b_M(q)$. By the definition of the unit quotient, there exists $e\in A^\times$ with $m=b_M(q)\iota(e)$. It is unique: equality $b_M(q)\iota(e)=b_M(q)\iota(e')$ cancels in $M^{\rm gp}$, and integrality of $M$ followed by injectivity of $\iota$ gives $e=e'$. Thus $(q,e)\mapsto b_M(q)\iota(e)$ is a bijective monoid homomorphism; its inverse is a homomorphism since the unique coordinates of a product are $(q+q',ee')$.

source.place: VI 1.1, printed p.69, and 3.7(a), printed p.75; agent unit-coordinate argument

proof.text: Step 6 gives characteristic $q$ for $\lambda(s(q))$. Applying Step 7 to it gives a unique $u(q)\in A^\times$ with $\lambda(s(q))=b_M(q)\iota(u(q))$. Both $\lambda s$ and $b_M$ are monoid homomorphisms. Multiplying their expressions at $q,q'$ and using uniqueness of the unit coordinate gives $u(q+q')=u(q)u(q')$, and at $0$ gives $u(0)=1$. This proves existence and uniqueness of the homomorphism $u$. Applying $\beta$ to its defining equation gives $c(q)=\alpha_F(s(q))=u(q)b(q)$. The assertion about $v$ was proved in Step 4.

source.place: VI 3.7(a), printed p.75; agent comparison of two lifts of the characteristic

proof.text: Every $q\in Q$ has a representative $r=p-f\in P_F$, and $\pi(r)=\pi(p)$ because $f\in G$; hence $P\to Q$ is surjective. If $\pi(h)\in H_x$ and $q=\pi(p)$, with $h\in H$ and $p\in P$, then $\pi(h)+q=\pi(h+p)\in H_x$. Thus $H_x$ is an ideal, also when $H$ is empty. Every $h-f\in H_F$ maps into $H_x$. Conversely, if $\pi(r)=\pi(h)$ for some $h\in H$, then $r-h=f_1-f_2$ for $f_1,f_2\in F$. Therefore $r=(h+f_1)-f_2\in H_F$ since $h+f_1\in H$. This proves $H_F=\pi^{-1}(H_x)$. In the coordinates of Step 3 the projection is $(q,g)\mapsto q$, so $H_F=H_x\oplus G$.

source.place: VIII 3.1.1--3.1.3, printed p.98; agent monoid-ideal calculation

proof.text: For naturality let $\rho:A\to A'$ and $\tau:M\to M'$ preserve the stated data, with $P,F,s$ fixed and $\tau a_M=a'_M$, $\tau b_M=b'_M$, $\beta'\tau=\rho\beta$. On units one has $\tau\iota(e)=\iota'(\rho(e))$, since applying $\beta'$ determines the unique unit lift. The formulas give $\rho\alpha_F(p-f)=\alpha'_F(p-f)$ and $\tau\lambda(p-f)=\lambda'(p-f)$, since ring homomorphisms preserve inverses of units. Each pushout representative $[r,e]$ maps to $[r,\rho(e)]$, so both pushout isomorphisms and their displayed inverses commute with these maps. The splitting in Step 3 uses only the fixed $P,F,s$, and its ideal subsets are the same ones for the fixed $H$. Finally applying $\tau$ to the defining equation for $u(q)$ gives the defining equation for $u'(q)$ with unit $\rho(u(q))$; uniqueness gives $u'(q)=\rho(u(q))$. The equations for $c$ and $v$ then commute with $\rho$ as well.
